facts.fact_text: The case concerns a protest against a preannounced eviction of a squatted building.
On 5 July 2011, at around 6 a.m., some 150 people gathered in front of and around the Schijnheilig squat at Passeerdersgracht in Amsterdam.

During the gathering on 5 July 2011 the participants danced, played instruments, stood close and talked to each other, and chanted slogans such as "Squatting's here to stay" and "You Government puppets".
Most of the participants in the gathering on 5 July 2011 were recognisable and wore plain clothes.
Some of the participants in the gathering on 5 July 2011 were dressed up in costumes or wedding dresses.
Some of the participants in the gathering on 5 July 2011 wore sunglasses, balaclavas or other masks or cloths to cover their faces.
The applicants argue that their arrest amounted to an unjustified interference with their right to freedom of peaceful assembly.
The applicants argue that their prosecution amounted to an unjustified interference with their right to freedom of peaceful assembly.
The applicants argue that their conviction amounted to an unjustified interference with their right to freedom of peaceful assembly.
At 8.37 a.m. on 5 July 2011 the Police Commissioner informed the participants that they were all under arrest.

A total of 138 persons, including the applicants, were arrested on 5 July 2011 on suspicion of participating in an unlawful gathering or otherwise disturbing public order, prohibited and made punishable by the Amsterdam general municipal by-law (Algemene Plaatselijke Verordening; the APV).

A total of 138 persons, including the applicants, were arrested on 5 July 2011 on suspicion of participating in an unlawful gathering or otherwise disturbing public order, prohibited and made punishable by the Amsterdam general municipal by-law (Algemene Plaatselijke Verordening; the APV).

On an unspecified date, the applicants were summonsed to appear before the limited jurisdiction judge (kantonrechter) of the Amsterdam Regional Court on suspicion of participating in an unlawful gathering or otherwise disturbing public order, contrary to section 2.2(1) of the Amsterdam general municipal by-law (APV).

On an unspecified date, the applicants were summonsed to appear before the limited jurisdiction judge (kantonrechter) of the Amsterdam Regional Court on suspicion of failing to comply with a police order to disperse, contrary to section 2.2(3) of the Amsterdam general municipal by-law (APV).

Section 2.2(1) of the Amsterdam general municipal by-law (APV) of 2008 prohibits, on or near the public road or in a building or vessel accessible to the public, participating in an unlawful gathering (samenscholing), defined in section 2.1(4) as 'a gathering of people who assume a threatening attitude, have malicious intentions or appear threatening', or, either as a member of a group or individually, imposing oneself unnecessarily, harassing others, fighting or otherwise disturbing public order (de orde verstoren).

Section 2.2(3) of the Amsterdam general municipal by-law (APV) of 2008 requires a person who is present on or near the public road at an event that attracts members of the public or at any occurrence that causes or is likely to cause disturbances (ongeregeldheden), or who is moving towards that event or occurrence, to immediately obey an order given by a police officer to move away in a given direction.

A total of 138 persons, including the applicants, were arrested on 5 July 2011 on suspicion of participating in an unlawful gathering or otherwise disturbing public order, prohibited and made punishable by the Amsterdam general municipal by-law (Algemene Plaatselijke Verordening; the APV).

The Amsterdam Court of Appeal held that the facts on 5 July 2011 led to a disturbance of public order on the entire Passeerdersgracht within the meaning of section 2.2(1) of the Amsterdam general municipal by-law (APV).
The applicants argue that they had no violent intentions.
The applicants argue that the interference with their right to freedom of peaceful assembly was disproportionate.
The message on www.indymedia.nl stated: "We expect that the Mobile Unit [Mobiele Eenheid; a special operations unit of the police] will arrive at 6 a.m."
The message on www.indymedia.nl stated: "The protest (manifestatie) will continue until the Mobile Unit come to their senses".
Using protective shields and wielding truncheons, the Mobile Unit advanced and cleared the area in front of the Schijnheilig squat.
Items such as beer bottles and a beer crate were thrown at the police during the events on 5 July 2011 at Passeerdersgracht.
Several smoke bombs were used during the events on 5 July 2011 at Passeerdersgracht.
There was a small fire during the events on 5 July 2011 at Passeerdersgracht.

The Amsterdam Court of Appeal noted that the group reacted to the Police Commissioner's orders en masse by yelling and screaming, and that bottles were thrown in the direction of the Police Commissioner's vehicle.
The Amsterdam Court of Appeal noted that the people in the group did not comply with the Police Commissioner's orders to disperse.

The Advocate General noted that the protection of Article 11 of the Convention does not lapse if some participants in the demonstration have violent intentions or if marginal or sporadic violent or other criminal behaviour is displayed.

The Supreme Court noted that according to settled case-law of the Court, Article 11 of the Convention does not protect 'a demonstration where the organizers and participants have violent intentions', citing Schwabe and M.G. v. Germany, nos. 8080/08 and 8577/08, ECHR 2011 (extracts).
